pr_title: Don't strip no log values from keys with special meaning
pr_body:
##### SUMMARY
Don't strip no log values from keys with special meaning. Fixes #70455


[click here for bot help](https://github.com/ansible/ansibullbot/blob/master/ISSUE_HELP.md)
<!--- boilerplate: shippable_test_result --->
Looks like the test failure is related to this change. Weird that's it's only OpenSUSE 15.
Why does any key need to be striped or masked? A key either has special meaning for Ansible or for the modules. Why should the keys be stripped or masked?

This is not fixing the issue #70455. The value of any no_log parameter will result in the renaming of any returned parameter that only contains the value as a sub string. It is ok to change the parameter if it completely matches the parameter name that was marked no_log, but not when it only contains a sub string of the parameter name or value.

With the current behaviour it is not possible to rely on any returned parameter if no_log is used.

The test failure is because keys returned by `package_facts` are `bytes`.
```
old_data.keys()=dict_keys([b'python3-pycrypto', b'libtirpc-netco..._0-0', b'python3-PyYAML', b'python3-setuptools'])
```
Please rethink the stripping in the current form. The possibility to get 'damaged' information returned because a user has chosen a bad password is making this unreliable and unpredictable.

For me, the whole concept of masking the `result` part of the module is completely wrong. If the module returns values that are sensitive, it is the module that should be fixed, it is not on Ansible to hide this values. The `no_log` should only be applied to the values of the `invocation` part, and never to the keys or results.

Every word might be used (for any valid or "not so smart" reason), and we might want, but can't stop users from using bad choices for values attributed to sensitive data.

With this change, you are not fixing the security issues (as the sensitive data is discoverable by the masked bits), and are potentially breaking every module that uses `no_log`.

I think since the change in behavior is in response to a CVE, that maybe would should not only not mask the key data but actually fail the task in this situation with an error message similar to the following:

```
Value of no_log data found to match key data, this no_log data is not longed even in key data because it
would log sensitive data or make it easily determined. This is likely the result of insecure no_log data
(such as a password) that easily matches common module result key names. This is not allowed because
it would break module return value subscripting.
```

Thoughts?

Ansible does not know if there is an overlap of sensitive and insensitive information only because a user has chosen a password that accidentally matches the name or parts of the name of a parameter. With the lack of this information it is not possible for Ansible to remove the sensitive information from returning parameters and values without also introducing unwanted and unexpected removals. In my opinion the CVE should have been addressed in the affected plugin instead.

If the user changes sensitive information like a password using an Ansible module, the user might not be able to change it again, because the module might be failing to return proper information or because it simply returns an error. Please also think about roles that are using several modules, where one is affected by this. How do you want to make sure that the role is gracefully handling this case?

@t-woerner I don't disagree that it's a module issue, the trouble is if that module comes from somewhere other than Ansible (embedded in a Role or from a Collection), it's still a CVE against Ansible and we get ding'd on it. That's just the reality of the situation we're in.

@maxamillion The only thing you could do is to add a pre check in Ansible to make sure that there is no possible overlap of the `no_log` parameters with returned parameters. But this depends on having these `no_log` parameters before starting the module, which is not working for roles where `no_log` parameters are generated on run time. Also this is not possible for returned values that accidentally match or partly match the `no_log` parameters.

How do you plan do handle modules that are returning `no_log` parameters as list of characters, reversed, extended or as base64 for example? There will always be a way to return `no_log` parameters.

> @maxamillion The only thing you could do is to add a pre check in Ansible to make sure that there is no possible overlap of the `no_log` parameters with returned parameters. But this depends on having these `no_log` parameters before starting the module, which is not working for roles where `no_log` parameters are generated on run time. Also this is not possible for returned values that accidentally match or partly match the `no_log` parameters.

That is, in fact, not the only option as has been discussed previously in this pull request. It is true that it is impossible to know all `no_log` values at the start of a playbook execution but this is exactly the reason for the proposal I made previously.

@maxamillion if you are talking about failing the task, it is slightly better than masking the output, but still would face the problem that a perfect valid task might fail if part of an encoded value (i.e. base64) matches the value of a `no_log` parameter.

> @maxamillion if you are talking about failing the task, it is slightly better than masking the output, but still would face the problem that a perfect valid task might fail if part of an encoded value (i.e. base64) matches the value of a `no_log` parameter.

Is there key data from a module that is base64 encoded that this is a concern for? also, we should be able to deal with encodings if we absolutely have to

> Is there key data from a module that is base64 encoded that this is a concern for? also, we should be able to deal with encodings if we absolutely have to

I don't know of any module now, but imagine something like an hexadecimal string, like Github's CLI key, that is used to retrieve a base64 encoded image from some service. The encoded image might contain a substring that matches the key value and thaan the task would fail. I know the odds on the example are pretty small, but it is similar to some sensitive data being returned in a URL for a badly written service or module.

What if there is an option for a module/task to opt-in or opt-out logging at all? So it places looging security on the modules or users?

@rjeffman you can 'opt out' right now, just don't use the provided functions for exiting a module, you'll have to handle JSON output yourself but that would bypass the sanitation. This is not built into core, just to the utility functions we share to make module development easier.

That said, we are discussing on other ways to handle this, but if you need a solution 'right now' .. you already have it.

@bcoca so does this mean that sanitizing output (i.e. masking it breaking the current contract) can be bypassed by handling the output without Ansible function, and returning the output for the controller, exiting again the reason this change has been made?

Doesn't this make all this change to hide the output useless, as the security issues will still be there?

Not useless, it just shifts it to YOUR code vs the project's code, there is no way for the controller to guarantee 3rd party modules are secure, only that the common code we supply is. 

Ansible can execute arbitrary 3rd party plugins you supply to it, in the case of modules, they don't even need to be Python, can be compiled or any other intepreted language, anything you can execute on the remote. For python and powershell we provide 'common code' to make it easier for authors, we are responsible for that code and any CVEs associated,  but not for 3rd party code

issue_context.title: Output is modified when module set no_log to True.
issue_context.body:
##### SUMMARY

When Ansible 2.10.0a1 under Azure there might happen that the output of a
task is changed if a module uses no_log = True for an attribute.

For example, if the output of the module should contain "changed: True", and
an attribute with no_log set contains the value `hang` it might happen that
the output is modified to "c******ed: True", and if this output is further
processed (registering the result and comparing the value of `changed`),
the test might fail, but not because of module code, but because of unexpected
output processing.

This behavior was, currently, only reproduced with Ansible 2.10.0a1 running
under Azure. I did not have 2.10.0b1 to test it.

##### ISSUE TYPE
- Bug Report

##### COMPONENT NAME

ansible output

##### ANSIBLE VERSION
2.10.0a1

##### OS / ENVIRONMENT
Controler: Ubuntu 18.04, on Azure
Targets: Centos 8.1, also on Azure

##### STEPS TO REPRODUCE

With a module that has a variable with "no_log" set to True, set the value of variable to `hang`, the output contains `c******ed: True`.

It was easy to reproduce with [ansible-freeipa](https://github.com/freeipa/ansible-freeipa) module ipavault.

##### EXPECTED RESULTS

If the value in the output is not part of the attribute, it should not be hidden.

##### ACTUAL RESULTS

Several string matching the attribute value in the output are modified to `******`.

This is expected.  We were made aware of a shortcoming in our `no_log` heuristics that could allow the `no_log` values to show up in keys, whereas previously we only restricted to values.  This was done in https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/69653 but was not backported for reasons of a backwards incompatible change made in a minor release.

If you have further questions please stop by IRC or the mailing list:

   * IRC: #ansible on irc.freenode.net
   * mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/ansible-project

The problem with this expected behavior is that if you have one single character in the field set to no log, you get an output like this:
```
ok: [cos81.ipa.test] => {
    "********hanged": true,
    "changed": false,
    "invo********ation": {
        "module_args": {
            "a********tion": "vault",
            "data": "VALUE_SPECIFIED_IN_NO_LOG_PARAMETER",
            "datafile_in": null,
            "datafile_out": null,
            "des********ription": null,
            "groups": null,
            "ipaadmin_password": "VALUE_SPECIFIED_IN_NO_LOG_PARAMETER",
            "ipaadmin_prin********ipal": "admin",
            "name": [
                "asymvault"
            ],
            "new_password": null,
            "new_password_file": null,
            "ownergroups": null,
            "owners": null,
            "ownerservi********es": null,
            "servi********e": null,
            "servi********es": null,
            "shared": null,
            "state": "present",
            "username": null,
            "users": null,
            "vault_data": "VALUE_SPECIFIED_IN_NO_LOG_PARAMETER",
            "vault_password": null,
            "vault_password_file": null,
            "vault_private_key": null,
            "vault_private_key_file": null,
            "vault_publi********_key": null,
            "vault_publi********_key_file": null,
            "vault_salt": null,
            "vault_type": null
        }
    }
}
```
Note that this output is actually **wrong**, as it says `ok`, but the correct result should be `changed`, as there were changes and they were reported by the module. The value of the field with `no_log` was set to `c`. Note that there are two entries for "changed" (`changed` and `********hanged`), with different values. The correct one here is the one that had the key name masked.
I do not understand why the no_log key name is replaced in all other keys as a sub string. I can understand that a key with the same name might be replaced though.

With the current behavior, I can even hide a failed module execution:

```yaml
  - name: Archive data value `data` to asymmetric vault
    ipavault:
      name: asymvault
      data: failed
      state: retrieved
``` 

The `data` attribute has `no_log` set, and this task should fail, but when I execute this, the result is "ok". If I change the value of data to be "foobar" it fails as expected.

If my module has a field ABC that is returned to the user, and the user password is "ABC", my module will not work because my key will be stripped.

Why strip key at all? What does it bring to improve security?
The password is not in the log, but having a look at the missing parts of the parameters reveals it. The parameter name or name part that is missing is the password.

Thank you.

The changes in #70762 seem to fix the problem.

review_comments: I don't understand the motivation behind stripping keys at all, I feel like this can conditionally break the contract defined by the `RETURN` structure of modules as documented. Is there a nuance I'm missing as to why that's desired/necessary?

As described in the previous issue, we were made aware that modules could return no_log values in keys.  In the example of the `uri` module, we have no control over the data format returned by the API, and as such, `no_log` data can appear in a key. Let's say that a module marks `user` as `no_log`, and the return of the module looks like:

We decided this was a security vulnerability.

That decision is not likely to be backed out.  However, what this attempts to achieve, is that this change doesn't step on assumptions by the ansible code base, specifically around whether or not a task can show up as changed/etc in the output.
This skips _modifying_ certain keys, not returning them. If a key contains a string that is in `no_log_strings`, we mask the value in the key not just the value.
Previously we only masked the value in the key, which could result in information disclosure if a `no_log` value ended up in they key.
You are revealing the no_log value with that. The missing part in the key is the password (no_log value).
Wait, so the original issue that was defined as a security vulnerability is that modules are exposing `no_log` data as a *KEY* in the past?

Also, if we're masking the string value of a *key* we're effectively breaking the data contract of the `RETURN` structure which will 100% break playbooks (as we've found out). This seems like a critical bug to me, I would instead suggest that if a key contains a `no_log` string then we should consider the module as failed with an error message as to why because it should be considered a bug in the module.
@maxamillion Yes, the `uri` module was getting a response back from an API that had username/passwords in the keys in the response (it was a substring of the key, not the entire key).

@samdoran that sounds like a but in the `uri` module ... is it possible for the introspection of the return data to check the `no_log` string and sanitize it's data in the module or error and provide a reasonable message?

I fear that swinging the hammer on the controller side like this is too heavy handed and will break a considerable amount of playbooks on accident. Granted, it might only be for CI or testing infrastructure were passwords are weaker and more likely that `no_log` data would accidentally match a key value but it's still going to be a game of whack-a-mole to keep adding "special keys" (I see this going sideways in Collections land). What I would propose is that a `no_log` value in a key is considered an error and the controller should fail the task with an appropriate error message and then module developers should handle this on their end, if possible.

@maxamillion I don't know that your idea of an error would be any more palatable to those involved here.  While right now you at least get something back, it would prevent the module from working at all for affected users.

@t-woerner it is the responsibility for the module to not leak information, but there have been CVEs against Ansible because `no_log` unintentionally leaked information because that responsibility was not upheld, so now there is oversight to attempt to ensure that it won't happen even if there's a module bug. We have to define a solution that allows that oversight to continue to function in a reasonable way. I'm open to options here but I think because of the history of CVE disclosures about this the Ansible dev community are large are sensitive to the issue.
